strengths: First test-time adaptation framework for vision-language object detectors (VLODs), addressing a genuine and previously unexplored gap; the related-work discussion carefully justifies this claim (e.g., Medeiros et al. 2025 requires labeled target data).

The two proposed components are well-motivated and detection-specific: IoU-weighted entropy exploits dense, overlapping proposals as free test-time augmentation and mitigates confirmation bias, while image-conditioned prompt selection addresses an empirically demonstrated failure of prompt averaging in VLODs.

Extensive and thorough evaluation: 6 benchmark datasets covering style, driving, illumination, and corruption shifts, plus PASCAL-C and COCO-C across severities, on two architecturally different detectors (YOLO-World, Grounding DINO), with consistent improvements over four adapted TTA baselines (TPT, VPT, DPE, Adapter).

Rich supporting analyses: ablations on prompt-generation strategies, adapter placement (with a plausible architectural explanation for YW vs. GD differences), hyperparameter sensitivity, batch size, augmentations, larger backbones, and pre-adaptation fine-tuning; complexity/FPS analysis with a favorable latency–accuracy trade-off.
Honest limitation discussion (underperformance on tiny low-overlap objects like Cityscapes) and clear presentation of the failure modes of standard entropy with motivating figures.
weaknesses: Moderate methodological novelty: both components are relatively straightforward—entropy minimization weighted by IoU-cluster size, and top-ρ prompt selection by mean logit—building on well-established ideas (TENT/TPT-style entropy, prompt ensembling, text-side residuals from DPE); the value lies mainly in the framework and empirical demonstration rather than a novel algorithmic insight.

Gains are modest in several settings (e.g., +1.0 mAP on driving scenes for YW, +0.5–1 mAP in some corruption families), and no error bars, variance estimates, or statistical significance tests are reported for any experiment, making small improvements hard to assess.

Evidence of dataset-dependent hyperparameter sensitivity: the optimal IoU threshold θ varies between ~0.5 and ~0.7 across datasets, and λ differs between detectors (0.3 vs. 0.1); it is unclear how these were selected without target-domain knowledge, which could raise concerns about the realism of the TTA setting.

Reliance on GPT-generated prompt pools introduces an LLM dependency that is not fully controlled; the ablation shows dataset-specific prompts give further gains but are excluded as unrealistic, yet the dataset-agnostic GPT prompts may still favor certain label vocabularies (e.g., PASCAL classes).

Minor inconsistencies and clarity issues: a ClipArt value appears as 45.4 (Tab. 1) vs. 45.2 (Tab. 6); the '96 distinct test scenarios' claim (Sec. 1) is not explicitly reconciled with the tables; the code link in the abstract is empty, weakening reproducibility; some standard-TTA comparisons (e.g., MEMO-style augmentation, EATA/anti-forget variants) adapted to detection are missing.

The single-step, per-image reset adaptation protocol, while practical, means the method cannot benefit from accumulating knowledge across the test stream; the interaction between this protocol and cache-based baselines like DPE (which do accumulate) deserves more analysis, particularly regarding whether IWE's advantage holds under online settings.

strengths: Claims the first test-time adaptation (TTA) framework for vision-language object detectors (VLODs), a genuine gap given prior TTA work targets either conventional ODs or VLM classification; the problem framing (proposal-level entropy minimization being ill-suited to detection) is well motivated.

The IoU-weighted entropy (IWE) objective is a sensible, detection-specific modification: weighting proposals by connected-component size in a class-wise IoU graph is simple, interpretable, and directly addresses confirmation bias from isolated/mislocalized boxes. The image-conditioned prompt selection (IPS) component is a reasonable fix to observed failure of prompt averaging in VLODs, supported by a dedicated ablation (Fig. 9, A.5).

Very extensive empirical evaluation: 6 datasets plus PASCAL-C/COCO-C corruptions (96 scenarios), two architectures (CNN-based YOLO-World and transformer-based Grounding DINO), three AP thresholds, and carefully adapted classification-TTA baselines (TPT, VPT, DPE, TENT-style adapters).

Strong supporting analyses: adapter-placement ablation, hyperparameter sensitivity (θ, γ, λ, ρ, M, batch size, augmentations), larger backbones (A.9), pre-fine-tuning effects (A.10), prompt-generation strategies (A.6), complexity/FPS analysis (A.4), and qualitative cluster heatmaps that illustrate the mechanism (A.13).
Honest limitations discussion: acknowledges underperformance on tiny-object-dominated scenes (Cityscapes) and reports cases where baselines marginally win (COCO-C specific corruptions).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: both components are largely heuristic combinations of known ideas (entropy minimization, graph/connected-component weighting, top-ρ prompt selection, adapter tuning, residual text offset from DPE). There is no theoretical or formal analysis of why the weighted objective reduces confirmation bias; the design choices (γ=1.1, θ=0.5–0.7, ρ=0.25, λ per-model) are empirical and show mild dataset dependence (e.g., θ peaks at 0.5 vs 0.7 depending on dataset), which weakens the plug-and-play claim.

Comparison with existing OD-TTA methods is missing: the paper cites STFAR (Chen et al., 2023), TeST, Yoo et al. (2023), Cao et al. (2025), and Ruan & Tang (2024) as related OD-TTA work, but only classification-TTA baselines are adapted for comparison. Adapting at least one established OD-TTA method to VLODs would substantially strengthen the claim that detection-specific structure (IWE) is needed.

Absolute gains are modest on some benchmarks (e.g., ~+1 mAP on Cityscapes/BDD100K for YW; single-step, per-image adaptation with parameters reset each image), and the method roughly halves throughput (20 FPS vs 89 ZS); the cost-benefit trade-off is discussed but per-image latency in realistic streaming settings is not analyzed.

Experimental evidence concentrates on style/illumination shifts; driving-shift gains are small and the paper's own conclusion concedes IWE underperforms on many tiny low-overlap objects, i.e., precisely the hard real-world cases for detection.

Reproducibility concerns: the abstract's code link is empty, and several key details rely on appendix summaries; also, main results use only the small model variants, with larger backbones confined to an appendix subset of datasets.

Missing uncertainty reporting: no variance/seeds or significance tests are provided despite per-image stochastic adaptation; several margins (e.g., DPE vs VLOD-TTA on some corruptions) are within plausible noise.
Presentation issues: contribution claims could be tempered (component novelty is incremental), and some motivation figures rely on single cherry-picked examples (Fig. 1, Fig. 2).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: to the authors' (well-substantiated) knowledge, this is the first test-time adaptation framework for vision-language object detectors, which is a clear and useful contribution to the field.

The two proposed components are well-motivated and detection-specific: (i) IoU-weighted entropy (IWE) exploits the dense proposal structure of OD as free test-time augmentation and targets confirmation bias from isolated/mislocalized boxes, and (ii) image-conditioned prompt selection (IPS) addresses the empirically observed failure of prompt averaging in VLODs. Both are supported by illustrative motivation figures (Figs. 1, 2, 11).

The empirical evidence is extensive and convincing: 6 detection datasets spanning style, driving, illumination, and corruption shifts, plus PASCAL-C and COCO-C (96 scenarios), across two VLOD architectures (CNN- and transformer-based) and two model sizes. Improvements are consistent over well-adapted baselines (TPT, VPT, DPE, TENT-style adapters).

The ablations are thorough and add value: adapter placement analysis (vision vs. text side per architecture), prompt-generation strategies, hyperparameter sensitivity for all four key parameters, batch size, augmentations, top-M proposals, pre-adaptation fine-tuning, and a complexity/FPS analysis (Table 3) showing favorable latency and parameter budget.

The paper is clearly written, the method is well-formalized, and reproducibility is supported by detailed implementation settings and a broad appendix; code is promised (though the link is currently empty).
weaknesses: The individual technical components are relatively simple: IWE is a fixed, non-differentiable weighting of the standard entropy loss based on connected-component size in an IoU graph, and IPS is a top-ρ prompt filter plus a linear fusion with the detector logits and a text-side residual. The novelty lies mostly in the combination and the detection setting rather than in deep methodological innovation, which limits conceptual impact.

There is no explicit ablation in the main text isolating IWE vs. IPS vs. their combination; the reader must infer component contributions, and the standard-entropy vs. IoU-weighted-entropy comparison is deferred to the appendix (A.13) with qualitative evidence only.

Gains on real-world driving domains (Cityscapes, BDD100K) are modest (e.g., +1.0 mAP on YW), and the authors acknowledge that IoU-weighted entropy underperforms on scenes with many tiny, low-overlap objects; the method is therefore best suited to large-object regimes, which narrows its practical scope.

No statistical significance, variance estimates, or multiple-run results are reported; TTA results with a single adaptation step and pseudo-label-driven objectives can be sensitive to randomness, and this is not addressed.

The claimed 'first TTA framework for VLODs' positioning should be more carefully qualified against concurrent/related work (e.g., Medeiros et al. 2025, which the paper itself cites as adapting VLODs, albeit supervised), and a comparison against augmentation-based OD-TTA (e.g., MEMO-style) baselines is missing.

Several hyperparameters (θ, λ, ρ, M, γ) are tuned per detector family, and the optimal IoU threshold is mildly dataset-dependent; the paper discusses this but offers no automatic or adaptive selection strategy.
The code link in the abstract is empty, which weakens the reproducibility claim at submission time.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored and practically relevant problem: test-time adaptation of vision-language object detectors, where only one prior method (TTAOD-F) exists; the paper positions itself clearly against this limited prior work.

The two proposed components (IoU-weighted entropy minimization and image-conditioned prompt selection) are simple, well-motivated, and grounded in an insightful observation: dense, overlapping proposals carry redundant spatial evidence that standard entropy minimization ignores, causing confirmation bias. The motivation figures (Fig. 1, 2) illustrate the failure modes convincingly.

Comprehensive empirical evidence: six domain-shift datasets, two corruption benchmarks (96 scenarios), two detectors spanning CNN and transformer architectures, plus comparisons against four adapted TTA baselines and the prior SOTA TTAOD-F. Gains are consistent across nearly all settings.

Thorough ablation and analysis: component ablations, adapter placement per architecture, prompt-generation strategies, batch size, augmentations, input resolution, larger backbones, a specialized domain (Aquarium), and an honest failure-case analysis on Cityscapes that identifies rider/person label overlap and small objects, with confirming ablations (class merging, higher resolution).

Favorable efficiency trade-off is demonstrated quantitatively (Table 5, 7): large memory and latency reductions relative to TTAOD-F (3.76 vs. 11.37 GB; 531.6 vs. 701.9 ms/img) with comparable or better accuracy, and the warm-start variant (VLOD-TTA*) strengthens the comparison fairly by adopting TTAOD-F's initialization strategy.

The supplementary material substantially strengthens the paper: hyperparameter sensitivity analyses, IoU-weighting shown to transfer to pseudo-label-based TTA (Table 6), and COCO-C/PASCAL-C results across all severity levels.
Limitations are acknowledged candidly (degradation on small-object scenes, latency above zero-shot due to backpropagation), which appropriately frames the contribution's scope.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is moderate. IoU/cluster-size weighting of an entropy objective and top-ρ prompt selection are straightforward mechanisms, and prompt/context selection shares spirit with existing TTA practice (e.g., TPT's confidence-based view selection). The contribution is more an effective combination and empirical finding than a new algorithmic principle.

The 'theoretical justification' in the supplement is only a trivial cosine-Euclidean equivalence; it does not actually justify the top-ρ selection rule, the image-level averaging over all N proposals (which conflates proposals from different instances), or why selection should beat averaging. A more careful analysis is missing.

Potentially problematic experimental protocol: hyperparameters (θ, γ, λ, ρ, M, learning rate) appear tuned on the same style-shift datasets used as main benchmarks, and sensitivity is evaluated on these same datasets; there is no held-out tuning/validation discussion. Multiple ablations (e.g., ordering augmentations 'in the order that performed best in preliminary tests') suggest test-set-informed design choices, which could inflate reported gains.

No error bars or statistical significance despite single-step, single-image adaptation being stochastic (graph construction, top-M selection); gains on some datasets are small (e.g., +0.6 mAP on Cityscapes at 640; +0.2 mAP over TTAOD-F average), making variance a concern.

The TTAOD-F comparison is limited to COCO-C with Grounding DINO only; it is not compared on the six main datasets, so the claim of outperforming the prior SOTA rests on a single benchmark family and an average difference of 0.2 mAP.

The adaptation resets parameters after each image, making this effectively per-image inference-time optimization rather than accumulating online adaptation; the paper's framing as 'online TTA' could be discussed more precisely, and implications (no cross-image accumulation of domain knowledge) deserve analysis.

Reproducibility concerns: prompts are generated with 'ChatGPT-5' without released prompt lists in the main text (only a pointer to supp examples), the code link is empty ('Code :'), and results depend on detector-specific design decisions (adapter types, placement) that require implementation detail.

Several presentation issues: typos ('experimentsacross', empty code link), and minor result inconsistencies (e.g., Table 4 shows batch-norm VLOD-TTA outperforming the adapter version on ClipArt mAP, slightly muddying the stated preference for adapters).

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: test-time adaptation for vision-language object detectors is a sensible and practical research direction, and the paper is well positioned against the single prior method (TTAOD-F).

The two components (IoU-weighted entropy minimization and image-conditioned prompt selection) are clearly motivated, simple to implement, and the proposal-overlap insight is intuitive and well illustrated by Figs. 1-2.

The evaluation is broad: two detectors, six domain-shift datasets, two corruption benchmarks, 96 scenarios, plus a large supplementary with hyperparameter sensitivity, adapter placement, backbone, resolution, prompt-generation, and failure-case analyses (e.g., the honest Cityscapes failure analysis in Sec. 6.3).

A favorable efficiency profile versus TTAOD-F is demonstrated (parameters, memory, latency) and the method works in a practical batch-size-1, single-step setting, which strengthens the deployment relevance of the contribution.
The supplementary ablation showing IoU-weighted pseudo-labeling also helps a mean-teacher scheme suggests the core idea generalizes beyond the proposed objective.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. IWE is a heuristic reweighting of the standard entropy objective (weight = connected-component size raised to a power in an IoU graph), and IPS is a top-ρ prompt filtering scheme; both are incremental over well-established techniques (Tent-style entropy minimization, prompt ensembling/selection). The 'theoretical justification' in the supplement reduces to the trivial cosine-Euclidean equivalence and does not substantiate why the heuristic should work.

Absolute gains over the strongest simple baseline (Adapter + Tent) are small and of uncertain significance: roughly +0.5 to +1.3 mAP on style-shift datasets, +0.3 to +0.9 on driving datasets, and only +0.2 mAP over TTAOD-F on COCO-C (26.2 vs 26.0). No error bars, variance over seeds, or statistical significance tests are reported, so 'consistently outperforms' is hard to verify at these margins.

Hyperparameters appear dataset-dependent (λ = 0.3 for YW vs 0.1 for GD; θ and γ optima vary by dataset; batch-norm requires per-dataset learning rates). It is unclear how values like θ, γ, ρ, M were chosen — if tuned on the test sets, the evaluation is optimistic; the paper does not discuss a validation protocol, which is important in TTA.

Comparison with the prior SOTA (TTAOD-F) is confined to one benchmark (COCO-C) with one detector (GD), under a different batch size (1 vs 4), and the headline accuracy claim over it is marginal; the stronger claim of superiority rests mainly on efficiency, which is fair but should be framed more cautiously.

Reproducibility is weakened: the 'Code :' field in the abstract is empty, prompts are generated by 'ChatGPT-5' (a non-deterministic, proprietary tool) without fully released prompt lists in the main text, and several details are deferred to a supplementary that cannot be verified.

Some internal inconsistencies and presentation issues: ClipArt AP50 for VLOD-TTA is 45.4 in Table 1/Table 3 but 45.2 in Table 9; the supplementary proposition is stated as if it were a meaningful justification; latency of VLOD-TTA is ~2.5x zero-shot, which somewhat undercuts the 'low overhead' framing relative to plain entropy baselines.

Method-design choices feel ad hoc rather than principled: parameters are reset after every image (so adaptation is effectively per-image), adapters are placed differently per detector based on post-hoc ablation, and the IoU-cluster weighting can suppress small but correct objects (acknowledged for large γ and small-object scenes), meaning the method's applicability depends heavily on proposal statistics of the target domain.
The societal-impact discussion is absent, and limitations are only briefly acknowledged in the conclusion; given the surveillance/autonomous-driving application context, this is a missed opportunity.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored and practically important problem: test-time adaptation for vision-language object detectors. The paper is well positioned relative to the single prior VLOD-TTA method (TTAOD-F), clearly articulating its computational drawbacks.

The proposed method is simple, well-motivated, and technically sound. IWE's use of IoU-graph connected components to weight proposal entropies is a clean, detection-specific way to counter confirmation bias, and IPS's image-conditioned prompt selection is a sensible replacement for prompt averaging. The cosine-Euclidean proposition justifying IPS is correct and helpful.

Comprehensive and well-organized empirical evidence: 6 domain-shift datasets plus PASCAL-C and COCO-C (96 scenarios), two detectors (CNN- and transformer-based), four adapted baselines, and extensive ablations covering components, adapter placement, prompt-generation strategies, batch size, augmentations, pre-adaptation fine-tuning, backbones, and a specialized domain (Aquarium).

Strong efficiency analysis (Table 5 and 7): tuned-parameter counts, GPU memory, and latency are reported, and the accuracy-efficiency trade-off versus TTAOD-F (26.2 vs 26.0 mAP with ~3x less memory and ~25% lower latency) is persuasive.

Honest limitations discussion, including an unusually thorough failure-case analysis on Cityscapes (rider/person label overlap, small objects and input resolution) with dedicated ablations, and acknowledgment that the method remains slower than zero-shot. This strengthens credibility.
Adaptation is per-image with parameters reset after each prediction and only lightweight adapters tuned, keeping the method broadly applicable to both YOLO-World and Grounding DINO.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is modest. IWE is essentially entropy minimization with connected-component-size weights, and IPS closely resembles prompt-selection ideas from the CLIP TTA literature; the contribution is more a well-executed adaptation of known ingredients to the detection setting than a fundamentally new algorithm. This is acceptable for an Algorithms/General submission, but the conceptual depth is limited.

Absolute gains are sometimes small and inconsistent across settings: e.g., YOLO-World gains on Cityscapes (+0.6 mAP) and BDD100K (+1.3 mAP) are marginal, and on some COCO-C corruptions VLOD-TTA only matches or slightly trails baselines. On GD some baseline gains (TPT, VPT, DPE) are within noise (~0.1-0.4 AP), so statistical significance/variance across test sequences is not reported anywhere.

Reproducibility is undermined by the empty 'Code:' link in the abstract; no code or prompt lists for the main experiments are available at review time. The method also depends on GPT-generated prompts (16 per class via ChatGPT), which introduces non-trivial implementation ambiguity that the supplement only partially resolves.

The TTAOD-F comparison has a confound: TTAOD-F runs at batch size 4 while VLOD-TTA uses batch size 1. The footnote discloses this, but batch size 1 degrades TTAOD-F's performance, and latency comparisons at different batch configurations are not strictly fair; a batch-size-matched comparison would strengthen the efficiency claim.

Latency of ~532 ms/img (GD) sits somewhat awkwardly with the framing of targeting 'real-time deployment settings,' and the single-step, single-image adaptation design raises questions about episodic/continual TTA settings (adaptation benefits do not accumulate), which is not deeply analyzed.

Minor presentation issues: a small numeric inconsistency between Table 9 (ClipArt AP50 45.2) and Tables 1/3 (45.4); typos ('experimentsacross', 'examines analyzes'); Table 5 mixes results from different batch configurations without isolating their effect on the reported memory/latency.
